H1.text: A football rolling slowly is easy to stop with your foot. A car rolling just as slowly is not.

H2.text: And a fast cricket ball stings your hands. So what decides how hard a thing is to stop?

H3.text: Diya waits at the college gate. A loaded truck creeps past. Inside, a cricket ball flies off a bat.

H4.text: The ball is forty times faster. The truck is far heavier. Which one is harder to stop?

H5.text: Speed alone cannot tell you. Mass alone cannot either. You need both, together.

P1.text: That combination has a name. Momentum.

P2.text: Momentum, p, is mass times velocity. p equals m v.

P3.text: Kilograms times metres per second. So momentum is in kilogram metres per second.

P4.text: Velocity has a direction, so momentum does too. More mass, or more speed, means more momentum.

P5.text: Newton called it the quantity of motion.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. A half kilogram ball and a two kilogram cart, on a smooth floor.

S2.text: Both move at two metres per second. The ball has one kilogram metre per second. The cart has four.

S3.text: Each body has its own line on the graph. The heavier body has the steeper line. The slope is the mass.

S4.text: Now send the ball at eight metres per second. Its momentum climbs to four. Exactly the cart's.

S5.text: Four times lighter, but four times faster. Same momentum.

S6.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, and draw the arrows.

S7.text: The blue velocity arrows are very different. Times the mass, the momentum arrows come out equal.

S8.text: Now stop both, in the same half a second.

S9.text: The orange stopping forces are equal too. Eight newtons each. Same momentum, same time, same force.

D1.text: Now let's link momentum to Newton's second law, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Momentum p equals m v.

D3.text: Step two. From episode fifty two, F equals m a, and a equals d v by d t.

D4.text: Step three. With the mass fixed, m d v by d t equals d by d t of m v. That is d p by d t.

D5.text: Step four. So F equals d p by d t. Net force is the rate of change of momentum.

D6.text: Step five. For a steady force, F equals the change in p over the time. Four over half a second is eight newtons.

D7.text: So F equals m a is the special case of fixed mass. And one newton second equals one kilogram metre per second.

T1.text: Remember this. Force is the rate of change of momentum.

K1.text: Side by side. The truck: ten thousand kilograms at one metre per second. Ten thousand kilogram metres per second.

K2.text: The ball: zero point one six kilograms, at forty metres per second. Just six point four.

K3.text: Now you try. Both must stop in one second. Which needs the bigger force? Pause and decide.

K4.text: The truck, by far! Same time, so the force follows the momentum. Ten thousand newtons, against six point four.

V2.text: A two kilogram cart rolls east at three metres per second. Take east as positive. p is plus six.

V3.text: Send it west. p is minus six. Same size, opposite direction. A different momentum.

V4.text: Your turn. Two kilograms east at three metres per second, or three kilograms west at two. Same momentum? Pause and decide.

V5.text: No! Both have a size of six, but plus six is not minus six.

W2.text: A twelve hundred kilogram van speeds up from ten to twenty five metres per second in five seconds. Find the change in momentum, and the net force.

W3.text: Starting momentum: twelve hundred times ten, twelve thousand kilogram metres per second.

W4.text: Final momentum: twelve hundred times twenty five, thirty thousand.

W5.text: So the change is eighteen thousand kilogram metres per second.

W6.text: Force is the change in p over the time. Eighteen thousand over five, three thousand six hundred newtons. Same as m a: twelve hundred times three.

X2.text: A thousand kilogram car moves at seventy two kilometres per hour. Many students write p equals a thousand times seventy two.

X3.text: But speed must be in metres per second. Seventy two kilometres per hour is twenty. So p is twenty thousand.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In questions that find p or its change, then the force.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A two kilogram body has momentum p equals four t squared, plus six t. Find the force and the acceleration at two seconds. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Twenty two newtons, and eleven metres per second squared.

A2.text: Force is d p by d t. That is eight t, plus six.

A3.text: At two seconds, eight times two, plus six, is twenty two newtons.

A4.text: Then a is F over m, eleven. Twenty eight is p itself, not the force.

Y3.text: Two. Why is momentum a vector?

Y4.text: Three. How does F equals d p by d t become F equals m a?
